It's strange because Middle Egyptian, which was purely hieroglyphic, was still around at this time; the Book of the Dead was written in Middle Egyptian.

Clement of Alexandria once made a testimony of hieroglyphs which Champollion used as a rudimentary guide to understanding hieroglyphs in the context of its use in Egyptian culture. She explicitly said that very few hieroglyphs were actually spoken aloud, and most were meant to be interpreted symbolically on one of three means of such interpretation. Granted this came out very close to the dissolution of ancient Egypt so it may have been an uninformed proposition, but it's certainly becoming clear that such claims may be true, especially with this new papyrus.

It never ceases to amaze me how ancient astronomers managed to gather the necessary information about such distant cosmic objects without all the neat little and not-so-little tools their modern colleagues have their disposal, even if their use of said information often seems rather trivial.
